The market for a normal good is in equilibrium at point X. Consumers' incomes fall and the cost of producing the good rises. In which area of the diagram will the new equilibrium be?
image: A standard supply and demand diagram. The vertical axis is 'price' and the horizontal axis is 'quantity'. An upward-sloping 'supply' curve and a downward-sloping 'demand' curve intersect at point 'X', representing the initial equilibrium. Four regions are labeled: 'A' (top right of X), 'B' (top left of X), 'C' (bottom right of X), and 'D' (bottom left of X). A fall in consumers' incomes for a normal good causes the demand curve to shift left. A rise in the cost of production causes the supply curve to shift left. Both shifts lead to a decrease in the equilibrium quantity. The effect on the equilibrium price is ambiguous, depending on the relative magnitudes of the shifts. Therefore, the new equilibrium could be in region B (higher price, lower quantity) or region D (lower price, lower quantity).
